title: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage
learningObjectives: Run SALT: global sort, lifesaving interventions, five categories including Expectant.
Compare START, SALT and Triage Sieve and know when each is used.
Tag correctly and re-triage at every hand-off point.
Explain over-triage vs under-triage and why both kill.

summary.title: SALT in 4 Moves
summary.content: SORT globally: 'Walk to me' (assess LAST), 'Wave/move' (assess SECOND), still or obvious life threat (assess FIRST). ASSESS individually and do LIFESAVING INTERVENTIONS (seconds only): control major hemorrhage, open airway (child: consider 2 rescue breaths), chest decompression (if trained), antidote auto-injector. Then: not breathing → DEAD. Breathing → ask 4 questions: obeys commands/purposeful movement? peripheral pulse? not in respiratory distress? major hemorrhage controlled? ALL yes → MINIMAL (minor injuries only) or DELAYED. ANY no → IMMEDIATE if likely to survive with current resources, otherwise EXPECTANT. TREATMENT/TRANSPORT by priority.

summary.title: Expectant (Gray) Is a Resource Decision
summary.content: Expectant = alive, but unlikely to survive given CURRENT resources (e.g., massive burns, devastating head injury with agonal breathing in a scene with 3 ambulances for 60 patients). They get comfort care and pain relief and are re-triaged as soon as resources allow — the same patient may become IMMEDIATE when the scene stabilizes. Expectant is not abandonment and not 'black'. START has no expectant step; SALT and many systems do.

summary.title: Which System?
summary.content: START/JumpSTART: simplest, widely taught in North America. SALT: CDC-sponsored national all-hazards guideline (adults and kids in one algorithm, includes LSIs and Expectant) — the basis of the Model Uniform Core Criteria. Triage Sieve (UK/NARU): primary triage by walking, catastrophic hemorrhage, airway, breathing rate, and pulse/CRT, ranking P1–P3. Secondary triage tools (e.g., Triage Sort using the Revised Trauma Score) are used at the treatment area. Use what your system trains — consistency beats elegance.

summary.title: Tags: Your Silent Radio
summary.content: Tags or ribbons tell everyone the category without a word. Minimum on a tag: unique number, category, time, and critical interventions (TOURNIQUET + TIME, antidotes given, decontaminated Y/N). Attach to a limb or neck — not clothing that will be cut off. Category changes: tear/fold the tag to the new color and note the time; never leave two contradictory colors. Use the tear-off stub for the transport log.

summary.title: Re-Triage and the Two Errors
summary.content: Triage is a snapshot. Re-triage at: primary (scene) → secondary (treatment area entry) → before transport → hospital arrival — and whenever condition or resources change. UNDER-triage (critical patient tagged low) causes preventable deaths. OVER-triage (non-critical tagged red) floods the red area and transport — critical mortality rises as over-triage rises (Frykberg). Trauma-system benchmarks: under-triage < 5%, over-triage ~25–35%. In MCIs, accuracy saves the reds.

clinicalPearls: SALT LSIs = 'Bleed, Breathe (airway ± 2 breaths for kids), Decompress, Dose (auto-injector)'.
SALT asks four YES questions: Obeys? Pulse? No distress? Bleeding controlled? Any 'no' → red or gray.
Write TQ + time on the tag (and on the patient's forehead if tags are short).
Same patient, different tag over time is normal — re-triage is the system working.
Over-triage feels safe but kills: it buries the true reds.
redFlags: Tags attached to jackets that get cut off in treatment.
Two colors on one patient with no time noted.
Expectant patients left alone without comfort care or re-triage.
No one assigned to re-triage the green area.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that walkers are assessed LAST, not skipped.
Forgetting the 2 rescue breaths for apneic children in SALT.
memoryAids: SALT = Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment/Transport.
Sort: Walk → last, Wave → second, Still → first.
Colors: Green walks, Yellow waits, Red runs (first), Gray gets comfort, Black is gone.
Tag must-haves: #, Color, Time, TQ/Antidote, Decon.

LSIs as needed: hemorrhage control | open airway (child: consider 2 breaths) | chest decompression | auto-injector
Breathing?
  → NO: DEAD

Obeys commands/purposeful movement? Peripheral pulse? Not in respiratory distress? Major hemorrhage controlled?
  → ALL YES: minor injuries only? YES → MINIMAL | NO → DELAYED
  → ANY NO: likely to survive with current resources?
        YES → IMMEDIATE | NO → EXPECTANT
Re-triage at every stage
